perspective:
Available to Mason Hurley:

- Mason works as an accountant at a small community center. Martha Moua is a colleague/personal care aide there; their relationship is professional and not personally close.
- Mason reviewed financial reports and observed discrepancies: healthcare expenses appeared unusually high and did not match usual spending patterns. This led him to suspect Martha might be mismanaging funds, making him suspicious and anxious.
- Mason asked Martha to discuss the report, saying numbers did not add up. He heard Martha say there was likely a reasonable explanation and ask which discrepancies he meant.
- Mason pointed to the healthcare expense section. He heard Martha say it might have been a misentry and that she would review and correct errors.
- After reviewing the report with Martha, Mason concluded the discrepancies were due to a simple clerical error, not mismanagement. He felt relieved and embarrassed.
- Mason told Martha he appreciated her quick clarification and said it seemed to be a clerical error. He heard Martha say errors happen, she was glad they cleared it up quickly.
- Mason apologized for his initial suspicion and said he should have asked her first. He heard Martha accept the apology, say she understood he was being thorough, and suggest double-checking entries next time.
- Mason came to believe Martha was competent, but that recurring clerical errors showed the current financial management system was inadequate. He felt frustrated with the system and empathetic toward Martha.
- Mason told Martha the issue was not her management but the current system. He proposed a new, more robust financial system and said he would draft a proposal and wanted her input. He heard Martha agree and offer to help address the gaps.
- Mason drafted the new financial system proposal. He was hopeful about its benefits but uncertain whether management would approve or implement it.
- Mason told Martha he had finished the draft, believed it would benefit operations, but was unsure how management would receive it. He heard Martha call it solid, encourage confidence, and say the benefits were clear.
- Mason said he would prepare a detailed presentation and asked Martha to help gather data. He heard Martha agree.
- Mason presented the proposal to management. He felt satisfied with his efforts but physically and mentally exhausted, believing he had done everything possible and that the decision was now up to management.
- Mason told Martha the presentation went well and it was up to management. He heard Martha praise his work, suggest taking time off, and say he deserved a break.
- Mason thanked Martha for her support and said he would take a few days off to recharge and reflect, hoping for good news. He heard Martha wish him a good break and offer help while he was away.
- Mason does not yet know management’s decision on the proposal.
